note: Which MWS requirements writecheck min mode judges against a mock of the backend made from its OpenAPI description. run: judged; a held needs the condition forced by the mock's own schedule (spec 8.2 rule 4). partial: only the half the mock can show is judged; it can give violated, never held (a held would rest on the half that needs a real backend). not_testable_mock: always reported not tested with status not_testable_mock and reason code backend_semantics_not_exercised, never held, never violated. One line per requirement says why. This file is the only list; src/min/requirements.ts reads it and a unit test checks it names all 37 requirements once.

MWS-UPD-1.why: Whether only the named fields changed is decided by the backend's merge semantics and a control arm (spec 8.2 rule 2: platform is listed); a mock merges by its own rule, so neither held nor violated is valid.

MWS-UPD-2.why: Landing on the element read at an address needs a second writer that inserts or reorders in a real store, and the control arm; a mock has no concurrent writer and its list semantics are its own.

MWS-CONC-1.why: The entry requires a control arm that shows the backend's concurrency control exists; a mock has no control of its own, so a bypass cannot be shown or ruled out.

MWS-CONC-2.why: A stale write is refused only if the backend detects it; a mock that never holds a second writer's version cannot force the condition, and a scripted 412 would test the reaction (MWS-CONC-4), not the precondition.

MWS-CONC-3.why: A lost update needs two writers interleaved against a store with real versions (held request or simultaneous pairs); a mock with one writer can show neither a loss nor its absence.

MWS-CONC-4.why: The mock answers a write that carried a precondition with the conflict status the description declares (412 or 409, deterministic); whether the result is isError, applied nothing at the mock, and says so is the server's own behaviour.

MWS-CONC-5.why: Review-only clause: the description declares which operations take no precondition (no If-Match parameter), which shows the backend cannot detect a stale write; the tool's description is then read with the declared pattern.

MWS-CONC-6.why: On the same forced conflict the mock returns the current object in the declared conflict body; whether the error carries that state or the declared re-read wording is the server's own behaviour.

MWS-TGT-1.why: Honouring a scope argument is judged against where the backend puts the object and a control arm (platform is listed); a mock files objects by its own rule.

MWS-TGT-2.why: The mock is a disposable store with a full inventory, so a call whose empty or missing selector removed or changed seeded objects is a valid violated; held would need the real backend's fallback for an empty selector, so it is never given.

MWS-TGT-3.why: Whether a create overwrites depends on the backend's duplicate handling and a control arm (platform is listed); a mock's answer to a duplicate is its own.

MWS-RES-1.why: Success only when the state asked for is in effect is read back from the backend's real effect (and the settle and in-flight forms need a real key store); a mock's effect is the mock's merge, so neither verdict is valid.

MWS-RES-2.why: Forced refusals, server errors and a lost answer after the mock applied the write are judged (isError, a false 'nothing was written', an invited blind repeat). The in-flight and settle forms need a real key store and concurrency, so the requirement is never held in min mode.

MWS-RES-3.why: The mock assigns the identifier of every object a call creates, so whether the result carries it, also when a later request of the call is failed on purpose, is the server's own behaviour.

MWS-RES-4.why: The mock knows the identifier and the version it returned for the write, so whether the receipt names them (and the shape, where the declaration adopts one, gives the version the mock returned) is the server's own behaviour.

MWS-ATOM-1.why: The mock fails the second item (or the batch, naming the second item) deterministically and records what it applied; comparing that with what the result reports per item is the server's own behaviour.

MWS-ATOM-2.why: All-or-nothing is a property of the backend's transaction together with the server; a mock's rollback is its own, so neither verdict is valid.

MWS-RETRY-1.why: Two identical calls of a create whose identifier the mock assigns make two objects at the mock (the description declares 201 only, so the backend does not dedupe them); whether the schema offers a key is read from the catalog.

MWS-RETRY-2.why: Key passthrough is observable at the mock, which honours the declared Idempotency-Key header: two objects for one key, a changed-argument repeat answered as a replay without reaching the mock, or a second create after a lost answer or a restart are valid violations. 'Answered with the first outcome' against a real key store is not, so the requirement is never held.

MWS-RETRY-3.why: The mock records every request the server sends before it returns input_required; a mutating request in that window is the server's own behaviour (proxy-assisted form).

MWS-IN-1.why: The server's own validation: the mock records the value the server forwarded for a wrong-typed probe, so a meaning-changing conversion is seen at the mock.

MWS-IN-2.why: An argument the schema does not define is either refused, forwarded (seen at the mock) or dropped; a drop without a declared notice is the server's own behaviour.

MWS-IN-3.why: A probe that breaks a declared constraint must be refused; a probe forwarded to the mock with a value the backend's own description accepts shows the server did not refuse it. A value the backend's description refuses is not judged (the real backend may refuse it).

MWS-IN-4.why: The error the server itself gives for a refused probe (no request reached the mock) is read for the argument name and the declared reason pattern.

MWS-IN-5.why: A schema-valid value refused with no request reaching the mock is the server's own constraint; violated rests on the declaration's fixed_constraints, as in full mode; without it the record is not tested.

MWS-IN-6.why: A wrong-typed probe accepted by the server (a call reached the mock) is the server's own conversion.

MWS-IN-7.why: An undefined argument accepted rather than refused is the server's own behaviour, seen without any backend semantics.

MWS-CFG-1.why: The server is started with each declared safety value; a write that reaches the mock under a restricting or unrecognized value is the server's own setting handling.

MWS-CFG-2.why: Started with an unknown name in the declared deny-list, the server must stop or disable writes; a write reaching the mock shows it did neither.

MWS-CFG-3.why: In the declared read-only mode every write tool is called; any write reaching the mock is the server's own setting handling.

MWS-CFG-4.why: Started with an unknown name in the declared allow-list, the server must stop; answering tools/list shows it did not.

MWS-ANN-1.why: A readOnlyHint tool that sends a mutating request to the mock changed state by the server's own request; a search over the calls made, so violated or not observed (spec 8.2 rule 8).

MWS-ANN-2.why: A destructiveHint: false tool whose request removed seeded objects or list elements it did not name is a valid violated at the mock; 'no change to data the caller did not name' against the real backend needs its state, so never held.

MWS-ANN-3.why: An idempotentHint tool whose repeat sends a second create the description declares as 201-only (a second object by the backend's own contract) is a valid violated; 'no further effect' otherwise needs the backend's state, so never held.

MWS-ANN-4.why: Read from the catalog: whether readOnlyHint and destructiveHint are declared explicitly needs no backend.

MWS-ANN-5.why: A destructiveHint: false tool whose request replaced or removed list elements at the mock is a valid violated; additivity against the real backend needs its state, so never held.

MWS-SEC-1.why: Every credential the server is given is a canary made for the run; a canary in any tool result, including the error results the mock provokes, is the server's own leak (violated or not observed).
